strengths: Novel approach combining meta-learning with test-time gradient descent on memory tokens; clean WRITE/READ decomposition with explicit optimization objective
Comprehensive synthetic benchmark (KV-retrieval) demonstrates clear advantages over forward-only writing, with consistent scaling across gradient steps
Well-motivated problem setup (context removal), clear presentation with excellent figures, and thorough appendices including computational analysis and efficient double-backward implementation

Strong technical execution: proper meta-learning framework (MAML), gradient descent formulation is sound, and ablation showing first-order approximations fail demonstrates appropriate use of second-order optimization
Honest treatment of limitations: discusses training overhead, when test-time compute is worthwhile (Section D), and provides code for reproducibility
weaknesses: Weak transfer to natural language tasks contradicts main contribution claims: SQuAD reaches 54.9% vs 64.2% for GPT-2 (~10% gap); bAbI QA3 achieves 79.3% vs 92.3% for ARMT; language modeling underperforms at 2.92 CE vs 2.72 for GPT-2, undermining task-agnostic reconstruction objective

Significant scalability concerns not adequately addressed: (1) all experiments on small models (4-layer to 160M parameters), (2) no analysis of training time overhead with double-backward through attention, (3) unclear feasibility on modern 7B+ models where second-order gradients become prohibitive

Limited practical applicability due to: (1) artificial context removal constraint (real applications like RAG have context access), (2) computational break-even requires ~60 queries per context (Equation 11, Figure 6), (3) large WRITE overhead limits single-query scenarios

Questionable baseline comparisons: RMT appears unexpectedly weak (19.3% on 32-pair KV-retrieval), fair comparison complicated by different memory architectures (per-layer vs single memory state), and limited comparison to other recent gradient-based compression methods (KV-Distill, ICAE, etc.)

Insufficient analysis of core design choices and assumptions: (1) no ablation on separate WRITE/READ heads or learned projections despite implementation details in Appendix B, (2) 'few-step regime' overstated as Figure 4 shows continued improvements far beyond training steps (K=30), (3) task-specific memory sizes (8 vs 32 tokens) lack justification

strengths: Clear technical execution with well-designed meta-learning formulation (inner loop on memory, outer loop on model parameters)
Fair controlled comparisons between gradient-based and forward-only writing using identical architectures and memory sizes, convincingly demonstrating scaling benefits
Thorough experimental analysis including scaling studies, computational latency measurements, and honest discussion of training overhead
Well-presented paper with informative figures and provision of source code for reproducibility
Sound technical approach to context compression through gradient descent optimization
weaknesses: Artificial and unmotivated problem setting: the 'context removal' constraint lacks justification for practical scenarios where standard KV-cache or other simpler compression methods suffice; no compelling use case presented

Weak performance on real language tasks: bAbI (80.0% on hardest task vs. 92.3% for ARMT), Short SQuAD (54.9% with increased K vs. 64.2% GPT-2), and language modeling results show full-context models significantly outperform compression approaches

Significant computational overhead with unclear payoff: expensive meta-learning requiring double-backward passes, plus substantial inference-time WRITE cost that only breaks even after ~64 READ operations; practical scenarios rarely meet these conditions

Limited novelty over prior work (particularly Sun et al., 2025 on TTT layers): both use test-time gradient optimization with self-supervised objectives; main differences are implementation details rather than conceptual innovations; few-step regime achieved primarily through meta-learning initialization

Overly simplified benchmark: KV-retrieval task doesn't reflect real language understanding; strong synthetic performance fails to translate to natural language tasks (QA3 underperformance suggests method struggles with high-information-density contexts)

Generalization concerns: single reconstruction loss across all tasks; fragile dependence on meta-learning (performance collapses without it); no evaluation on truly long-context scenarios (full documents, codebases) where compression is most critical

strengths: Clear and well-motivated approach with clean WRITE/READ decomposition and useful meta-learning perspective enabling memory writing in few gradient steps
Strong synthetic benchmark results on associative KV-retrieval demonstrating gradient-based writes substantially outperform forward-only writes at identical memory size (86.9% vs 45.5% on 32 pairs)
Key insight that additional gradient steps reliably scale memory capacity while repeated forward passes yield weak/inconsistent gains is valuable and well-demonstrated (Table 1)
Thorough experimental evaluation with good ablations, sensitivity analyses, and decomposition of what information is retained (Figure 8 shows selective value compression)
Comprehensive computational analysis including theoretical break-even conditions (Eq. 11), measured latencies (Figure 7), and practical guidance on when method is worthwhile
Implementation innovations including custom double-backward for attention that reduces GPU memory substantially (Appendix C) are valuable contributions
Reproducibility well-supported: code available, detailed hyperparameters, multiple runs with error bars, clear ablations demonstrating meta-learning necessity
Honest discussion of limitations and computational trade-offs; well-written with effective visualizations
weaknesses: Mixed and sometimes underperforming results on downstream NLP tasks: GradMem-K=1 achieves 80% on bAbI QA3 vs RMT's 87.9%, ARMT outperforms on language modeling (2.85 vs 2.92 CE), SQuAD results well below full-context upper bounds; claims of 'transfer beyond synthetic benchmarks' appear overstated given these results

Limited practical applicability: context-removal setting is clean for evaluation but artificial—most deployed LLMs have access to context; computational break-even requires 64+ queries per context (Figure 6), not all applications have this pattern

Significant training computational overhead requiring backpropagation through K unrolled optimization steps using second-order gradients; paper notes first-order approximations fail but provides insufficient analysis of why; limits scalability to larger models

Limited scaling demonstrations: largest model 160M parameters, longest sustained experiments ~256 tokens, KV-retrieval uses toy 4-layer models; no experiments on truly long contexts (>1k) or modern large models, limiting evidence of practical utility

Reconstruction loss acknowledged as suboptimal for downstream tasks, yet no experiments with alternative WRITE objectives (task-specific, contrastive, etc.); task-agnostic objective doesn't capture task-relevant information, limiting generality

Incomplete analysis of failure modes: no explanation for underperformance on bAbI QA3 or why ARMT beats GradMem on LM; limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis despite α being task-dependent; some experimental choices (separate heads, learned projections) appear ad-hoc

Baseline comparisons could be more comprehensive: ARMT uses per-layer memory interface (different from GradMem's single memory state), making direct comparison difficult; missing comparisons with simpler alternatives (end-to-end encoders, learnable prompt compression, recent KV compression methods); no ablation varying M_0 initialization

Test-time extrapolation generalization unclear: Figure 4 shows K_eval > K_train improves performance but limited analysis of extrapolation robustness, generalization to out-of-distribution contexts (much longer than training), or how far extrapolation can be pushed

strengths: Clear technical contribution with sound methodology: gradient-based WRITE operations are more expressive than forward-only alternatives, properly implemented with MAML-style meta-learning
Convincing synthetic experiments on KV-retrieval with clean benchmark: Table 1 demonstrates K=1 outperforms forward-only methods; Figure 4 shows consistent scaling with more gradient steps

Thorough experimental evaluation: multiple datasets (synthetic + NLP), extensive ablations (memory-K tradeoffs, input vs per-layer memory, comparisons to TTT-Linear/LaCT), analysis of learned representations (selective value retention)
Excellent reproducibility: code available, minimal code example, detailed implementation details (Appendix B), documented custom optimizations (Appendix C), complete hyperparameter specifications

Honest treatment of limitations: clearly analyzes when GradMem is compute-efficient (break-even analysis), discusses applicability constraints, acknowledges reconstruction objective may not be optimal for all tasks

Good technical soundness: proper second-order meta-learning with thorough ablations showing importance (w/o 2nd-order ablation in Table 1), fair comparison to RMT baseline with identical architecture/memory size
weaknesses: Limited practical impact on NLP tasks: Table 2 shows mixed results with GradMem matching or underperforming RMT; notably on QA3 GradMem significantly underperforms (80.0% vs 87.9% for RMT), and language modeling improvements are marginal (2.92 vs 2.91)

Significant computational training overhead: requires custom double-backward kernels through attention, curriculum learning needed for stability, second-order meta-learning is expensive and critical (Table 1 ablation), limiting scalability and adoption

Restricted applicability: method only beneficial when context reused multiple times (break-even can require tens to hundreds of queries), requires c >> m, thus limited to specific scenarios; not a general-purpose compression method

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: no investigation of why GradMem underperforms on QA3 despite task-agnostic objective; limited testing on diverse domains beyond synthetic+NLP; no analysis of behavior on very long contexts (>1024 tokens)

Design choices lack principled justification: Appendix J shows per-layer memory with 8× more parameters outperforms input-level memory, suggesting memory parameterization choice driven more by parameter budget than principled design; reconstruction loss selection acknowledged as suboptimal but minimally explored

Limited evidence of scalability to large models: Appendix I tests only 1B-3B models on very short spans (8-64 tokens) with LoRA adapters; main results on 100M scale; scalability to 7B+ models not demonstrated

strengths: Technically sound meta-learning framework with proper inner/outer loop formulation and comprehensive ablations demonstrating effects of K, memory size, and meta-learning signal
Strong synthetic benchmark results on associative KV-retrieval showing gradient-based memory updates consistently outperform forward-only methods and scale effectively with additional WRITE steps
Excellent technical execution including efficient second-order differentiation through attention (Appendix C) and clean separation of memory from model weights
Well-organized paper with comprehensive appendices, reproducible code, and detailed implementation details enabling reproducibility
Clean evaluation setting (context removal) that isolates memory writing capability and provides direct measure of information storage capacity
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily recombines existing techniques (TTT layers, MAML-style meta-learning, reconstruction loss) into a model-level architecture. The core ideas are well-established; main contribution is organizational rather than conceptual

Significantly overstated transfer to NLP: abstract claims 'competitive results on natural language tasks' but Table 2 shows mixed performance—underperforms RMT on bAbI QA3 (80.0% vs 87.9%), modest SQuAD gains (54.9% vs 64.2% full model), and negligible K-benefit on language modeling (2.92 vs 2.91 CE)

Reconstruction objective fundamentally misaligned with downstream tasks: paper acknowledges this limitation but provides no solution. Flat performance with increasing K on language modeling suggests learned representations don't capture task-relevant structure

Critical practical limitations under-emphasized: (1) training requires expensive second-order differentiation through K steps; (2) inference benefits only appear after ~64 queries per context (Appendix D); (3) single-query scenarios favor simpler KV-cache. These constraints should be in main text, not appendix

Unfair experimental comparisons: GradMem (1,024 params) vs TTT-Linear (17k) vs LaCT (49k)—this parameter efficiency advantage is substantial but obscures fair comparison. Appendix H shows LaCT best-of-3 runs (91.6% at 64 pairs) are competitive with GradMem-K=5 (99.1%)

Fundamental memory capacity limits: Figure 10 demonstrates increasing K only partially compensates for small memory size. At 16 KV-pairs, near-perfect performance still requires m≥4 tokens, suggesting gradient optimization cannot overcome information bottlenecks

Insufficient analysis of when to use this method: no guidance on practical scenarios where GradMem is preferable to alternatives (KV-cache with reuse, prompt compression, TTT-Linear, LaCT). Amortization requirement severely limits applicability

Limited exploration of alternative write objectives: despite acknowledging reconstruction is suboptimal, paper provides only brief discussion (Discussion section) with no systematic investigation of task-specific objectives that might better preserve task-relevant information

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation with intuitive WRITE/READ decomposition that directly measures compression capability

Strong and convincing synthetic results: GradMem stores 2x more KV-pairs than forward-only RMT baseline with same memory size; gradient updates scale consistently while repeated forward writes provide weak/inconsistent gains

Rigorous experimental methodology with well-chosen baselines (Mamba, RMT, ARMT, TTT-Linear, LaCT), multiple ablations (2nd-order meta-learning, input vs. per-layer memory), and careful measurement of variance

Novel technical contribution combining test-time gradient optimization of memory tokens with meta-learning, enabling few-step (K≤5) context encoding with explicit per-example error correction feedback
Thorough computational analysis with detailed break-even calculations (Appendix D) and measured latency comparisons (Figures 7-8) demonstrating practical efficiency tradeoffs across context lengths
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, custom optimization techniques explained, minimal code examples provided, code release promised
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations including training overhead, inference latency requirements, and suboptimality of task-agnostic reconstruction objective
weaknesses: Severe training computational overhead with second-order meta-gradients and custom double-backward attention implementation limits scalability; main experiments use small models (4-layer Llama, GPT-2-124M) and authors resort to increasing K only at inference rather than during training due to computational burden

Mixed results on natural language tasks undermine transfer claims: bAbI QA3 performance (80.0%) trails RMT (87.9%), WikiText language modeling shows no improvement over baselines (2.91 CE), and SQuAD gains are modest and K-dependent

Inference latency is prohibitive for single-query scenarios; break-even analysis (Appendix D) shows GradMem requires ~4-5 repeated queries per context to outperform caching, severely limiting applicability in typical use cases

Task-agnostic reconstruction objective is acknowledged as suboptimal but not addressed; Figure 4(b) reveals the model selectively reconstructs values over keys despite identical WRITE objective, suggesting generic compression misses task-relevant structure

Limited scaling evidence to realistic settings: text reconstruction (Appendix I) differs from actual downstream tasks; no full-scale experiments on instruction-tuned LLMs; contexts <256 tokens don't demonstrate long-context scaling claimed in motivation

Extreme dependence on second-order meta-learning: performance collapses from 99.7% to 12.9% without it (Table 1), indicating brittleness; unclear if 1st-order alternatives (iMAML, Reptile) were adequately explored

Natural language task evaluation is narrow (only QA and language modeling) and somewhat artificial (Short SQuAD restricts to answer-containing sentence); no classification, structured prediction, or other task families tested

Comparison fairness concerns: ARMT uses per-layer distributed memory while GradMem uses fixed input-level budget; Mamba's architecture-native state makes direct comparison difficult; different training procedures across methods
